details.actual:
The possible outcomes for each child are  

- Boy born on Monday, Tuesday, …, Sunday (7 possibilities)  
- Girl (any day) (7 possibilities)  

Hence each child has 14 equally likely possibilities and the ordered pair of children has  

\[
14 \times 14 = 196
\]

equally likely outcomes.

---

### Count the outcomes where “at least one child is a boy born on Tuesday”

* Exactly one child is a boy‑Tuesday: choose the child (2 ways) and the other child can be any of the other 13 possibilities → \(2\cdot13 = 26\) outcomes.  
* Both children are boys‑Tuesday: 1 outcome.

Total with at least one boy‑Tuesday:

\[
26+1 = 27.
\]

---

### Count the favorable outcomes (both children are boys)

If both are boys, each child can be a boy on any of the 7 days → \(7\times7 = 49\) outcomes.

We need those with **at least one boy‑Tuesday**:

\[
49 - (\text{no Tuesday boy}) = 49 - (6\times6) = 49-36 = 13.
\]

---

### Compute the conditional probability

\[
P(\text{both boys}\mid \text{at least one boy‑Tuesday}) 
= \frac{13}{27}.
\]

\[
\boxed{\frac{13}{27}}
\]

Assuming “one of them is a boy born on a Tuesday” means **at least one** child has that description:

- There are \(14\) equally likely sex–day combinations per child.
- Total two-child outcomes with at least one Tuesday-born boy:
  \[
  14^2-13^2=27.
  \]
- Outcomes where both are boys and at least one was born Tuesday:
  \[
  7^2-6^2=13.
  \]

Therefore, the probability is

\[
\boxed{\frac{13}{27}}.
\]

details.actual:
With the usual abuse of language the 2 children
are {\it a priori}

$$14\times 14=196$$

equally likely.

Put for one birth

$$P(B)=P(G)=1/2\qquad P(T\mid B)=1/7$$

and assume independence in sex , in day and between
the two births.  For one birth

$$P(BT)=1/14,\qquad P(B\bar T)=6/14,\qquad P(G*)=7/14$$

so that for one birth

$$P(\overline{BT})=13/14 .$$

For $2$ (ordered) births

$$P({\rm no\;}BT)=(13/14)^{2}=169/196 .$$

Hence in the ordinary set theoretic sense

$$A:={\rm ``\ge 1\;child\;is\;}BT$$

$$P(A)=1-169/196 =27/196 \tag{1}$$

about $13.8\%$ of $2$ child families.

$$B:={\rm ``2\;boys''}$$

$$P(B)=1/4\qquad 49 {\rm \;ordered\;day\;combinations.}$$

$$B\cap A = {\rm ``2\;boys\;and\;\ge 1\;T''}$$

$$P(B\cap A)= P(B)-P(B\bar T B\bar T)=\frac14 -\left(\frac12\frac67\right)^{2}
 =\frac{49-36}{196}= \frac{13}{196} \tag{2}$$

Indeed of the $49$ $BB$ day combinations $36$ are
$\bar T\bar T$.

Hence, {\it conditioned on the family belonging to the
set $A$},

$$P(B\mid A)=\frac{P(B\cap A)}{P(A)}=\frac{13/196}{27/196}
      =\frac{13}{27}\approx 0.48 $$

in lowest terms.

*  $13$ ordered possibilities for $BB$ with $\ge 1T$;
*  $14$ ordered possibilities for $BG$ or $GB$ with the
$B$ on $T$: $7+7$.

$27$ ordered $BT$--families in all.

Neglecting the $T$ you get the usual $1/3$, $1$ $BB$ in
$3$ $B*$ families.  The $T$ favours $BB$, which has two
chances to hit $T$, so the $1/3$ is raised to $13/27$.

In the limit of a very rare $T$, $P(T)=p\to 0$,
$P(B\mid A)\to 1/2$.

> {\it Remark on language:} That is $P(B\mid A)$ for the
> collective existential {\it ``the family has $\ge 1\,BT$''}.
> If you learn the property from a {\it distinguished} child,
> e.g. a child met at random is $BT$, or a child chosen
> at random from the family to describe is $BT$, the
> ordinary Bayesian update is $1/2$.  Up to $13/27\approx
> 1/2$ the difference is normally glossed over.

Indeed put $R=$ {\it ``a random child of the family
reported to you is $BT$''}.  Then $P(R\mid BB)=1/7$,
$P(R\mid BG)=P(R\mid GB)=1/14$, $P(R\mid GG)=0$, so

$$P(R)= \tfrac14\tfrac17+\tfrac12\tfrac1{14}=1/14,\;
  P(B\cap R)=1/28$$

and

$$P(B\mid R)=1/2$$

in the usual sense.  In particular if ``one of them''
means a {\it particular} one of them - the oldest,
the one you met, etc. - is $BT$, the chance the other
is a boy is $1/2$.
